subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: 1.1 Scalars and Vectors in One Dimension
1.5 Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions

questions.q: Two carts move along the same straight track, with the positive direction to the right. Cart 1 has velocity +3 m/s and cart 2 has velocity −3 m/s. Which statement correctly compares the two carts?
options: Their velocities are equal, since each of the two velocities has the same magnitude, 3 m/s.
The speeds of carts 1 and 2 are equal, but their velocities differ in direction.
Cart 2 has the smaller speed, since its velocity is a value less than zero.
Cart 2 is slowing down but cart 1 is not, since cart 2's velocity is the negative one.
optionWhy: A student who compares vectors by magnitude alone picks this. Two vectors are equal only if they have the same magnitude AND the same direction; these velocities point in opposite directions.
Speed is a scalar, the magnitude of velocity, so both carts move at 3 m/s. Velocity is a vector: the opposite signs show that the carts move in opposite directions, so their velocities are different.
A student who reads −3 m/s as a smaller quantity than +3 m/s picks this. The minus sign gives only the direction; the magnitude of −3 m/s is 3 m/s, so the two speeds are equal.

A student who reads a negative velocity as slowing down picks this. The sign says only that cart 2 moves to the left; one velocity value for each cart says nothing about whether either speed is changing.
questions.explain: Speed is a scalar, the magnitude of velocity, so both carts move at 3 m/s. Velocity is a vector: the opposite signs show that the carts move in opposite directions, so their velocities are different.
questions.working: Speeds: |+3 m/s| = |−3 m/s| = 3 m/s, so the speeds are equal. Velocities: +3 m/s (to the right) and −3 m/s (to the left) have the same magnitude but opposite directions, so the velocities differ.

questions.q: A student records four facts about a school bus trip. Which fact describes a vector quantity?
options: The whole trip lasted for a total time of 2 hours.
The temperature outside at noon was −3 °C.
The bus's speedometer read 60 km/h at noon.
The bus ended the trip 30 km east of the school.
optionWhy: A student who thinks time is a vector because it 'runs forward' picks this. Two hours is described completely by a magnitude and a unit; it has no direction in space, so time is a scalar.
A student who thinks any quantity that can be negative is a vector picks this. −3 °C is a value below the zero of a temperature scale, not a direction in space; temperature is a scalar.
A student who treats speed and velocity as the same quantity picks this. A speedometer shows speed, the magnitude of the velocity with no direction, so its reading is a scalar.
'30 km east of the school' gives a magnitude (30 km) and a direction (east) measured from a chosen origin, the school. It is the bus's final position, a vector.
questions.explain: '30 km east of the school' gives a magnitude (30 km) and a direction (east) measured from a chosen origin, the school. It is the bus's final position, a vector.
questions.working: 30 km east of the school has a magnitude and a direction relative to an origin (a position). 2 hours (time), −3 °C (temperature) and 60 km/h (a speed) have magnitudes only.

questions.q: A cart moves along a straight track that lies along the x axis. A textbook writes the cart's velocity as v⃗ in one equation and as v_x in another. Which statement about these two symbols is correct?
options: v⃗ is the velocity vector; v_x is its component along x, whose sign gives the direction.
v⃗ and v_x name the same quantity, so the arrow may be written or left off at will.
v_x is the magnitude of v⃗, so it is the cart's speed and cannot have a negative value.
v_x can take negative values, so it is a vector and has to be written with an arrow.
optionWhy: The arrow marks v⃗ as a vector, with a magnitude and a direction. For motion along one axis the vector is described by its component v_x, a signed number whose sign gives the direction, so v_x needs no arrow.
A student who thinks the arrow is decoration picks this. The arrow marks a vector; v_x is a component, a signed number along one axis. Writing v⃗ = 12 m/s, for example, leaves out the direction.
A student who treats a component as a magnitude picks this. The magnitude of v⃗, the speed, is never negative, but the component v_x is negative whenever the cart moves in the −x direction.

A student who thinks every signed quantity needs vector notation picks this. v_x does take negative values, but it is a component along an axis, and vector notation is not required for components: the sign alone gives the direction.
questions.explain: The arrow marks v⃗ as a vector, with a magnitude and a direction. For motion along one axis the vector is described by its component v_x, a signed number whose sign gives the direction, so v_x needs no arrow.

questions.q: In the diagram, the top arrow represents a velocity of +2 m/s, with the positive direction to the right. Arrows A–D are drawn to the same scale. Which arrow represents a velocity of −6 m/s?
options: Arrow A
Arrow B
Arrow C
Arrow D
optionWhy: A student who drops the minus sign picks this. This arrow has the right length, three times the reference, but it points to the right, so it represents +6 m/s. In one dimension the sign of a component is its direction.

A student who thinks an arrow's length is arbitrary picks this. It points the right way but is the same length as the +2 m/s arrow, so it represents −2 m/s; a 6 m/s velocity needs an arrow three times as long.

−6 m/s has a magnitude of 6 m/s, three times the magnitude of the +2 m/s reference, and its minus sign means it points in the negative direction. The correct arrow points to the left and is three times as long as the reference arrow.

A student who thinks −6 m/s is a smaller quantity than +2 m/s picks this. It points to the left but is shorter than the reference, so it represents only −1 m/s. The magnitude of −6 m/s is 6 m/s, three times the reference.
questions.explain: −6 m/s has a magnitude of 6 m/s, three times the magnitude of the +2 m/s reference, and its minus sign means it points in the negative direction. The correct arrow points to the left and is three times as long as the reference arrow.
questions.working: |−6 m/s| ÷ |+2 m/s| = 3, so the arrow must be three times as long as the reference arrow; the minus sign means it points in the negative direction, to the left. Only C is three times as long and points left.

questions.q: A student is asked for the average velocity of a 200 m long train that travels 150 km along a straight track between two cities. She decides to model the train as an object. Which statement about her choice of model is correct?
options: It is unsuitable, since an object as large as a train cannot be treated as a point.
It is suitable, provided the train is given no mass, since a point has no size.
It is suitable, since the train's size and shape do not affect the answer.
It is unsuitable, since the train's front and back are at different positions.
optionWhy: A student who thinks only small objects can be modeled as points picks this. What matters is whether size affects the quantity asked for; here it does not, so even a train can be treated as an object.
A student who thinks a point has no mass picks this. The object model ignores size and shape but keeps extensive properties such as mass: the point has the whole mass of the train.

In the object model, size, shape and internal configuration are ignored. The train's 200 m length is small compared with the 150 km trip, and every part of the train has the same displacement, so treating it as a single point does not change its average velocity.

A student who thinks an extended object has no single position picks this. The front and back of the train are at different places, but they have the same displacement, so one point represents the train's motion.
questions.explain: In the object model, size, shape and internal configuration are ignored. The train's 200 m length is small compared with the 150 km trip, and every part of the train has the same displacement, so treating it as a single point does not change its average velocity.

questions.q: Swimmer A swims one 50 m length of a straight pool and stops at the far end. Swimmer B swims two lengths, to the far end and back, and stops where she started. Which statement correctly compares the two swimmers?
options: B's displacement is greater, since B swam twice as far as A.
Their displacements are equal, as both got 50 m from the start.
B's displacement is negative, as B was swimming back at the end.
A's displacement is greater, but B swam the greater distance.
optionWhy: A student who treats displacement as the distance traveled picks this. B swam 100 m, but she ended where she started, so her displacement is zero.
A student who takes displacement to be the farthest distance reached picks this. Both reached the far end, but B came back: displacement uses only the final position, so B's is zero.

A student who gives the displacement the direction of the final motion picks this. B was moving back toward the start at the end, but she finished exactly where she started, so her displacement is zero, neither positive nor negative.
Displacement depends only on the start and finish: A's is 50 m toward the far end, and B's is zero, since she ends where she started. Distance is the path length: 50 m for A and 100 m for B.
questions.explain: Displacement depends only on the start and finish: A's is 50 m toward the far end, and B's is zero, since she ends where she started. Distance is the path length: 50 m for A and 100 m for B.

questions.q: Cars 1 and 2 both leave town P at 1:00 p.m. and arrive at town Q, 60 km away along a straight road, at 2:00 p.m. Car 1 travels at a steady speed. Car 2 stops for 10 minutes on the way and drives faster than car 1 for the rest of the trip. Which statement about the cars' average velocities for the trip is correct?
options: They are equal: cars 1 and 2 have the same displacement in the same time.
Car 1's is greater, since car 2 was not moving for part of the trip.
Car 2's is greater, since car 2 reached a greater top speed than car 1 did.
They cannot be compared without car 2's velocity at every instant.
optionWhy: Average velocity is Δx/Δt, which depends only on the initial and final states. Both cars have a displacement of 60 km toward Q in the same 1 h interval, so both have an average velocity of 60 km/h toward Q.
A student who treats average velocity as the typical velocity while moving picks this. Car 2 makes up for the stop by driving faster, and it still has the same displacement in the same time interval.
A student who thinks the top speed sets the average picks this. Car 2's higher speed only makes up for its stop; its displacement and time interval are the same as car 1's.
A student who thinks an average needs every value picks this. An average velocity needs only the displacement and the time interval, and both are given.
questions.explain: Average velocity is Δx/Δt, which depends only on the initial and final states. Both cars have a displacement of 60 km toward Q in the same 1 h interval, so both have an average velocity of 60 km/h toward Q.
questions.working: Both cars: Δx = 60 km toward Q and Δt = 1 h (1:00 p.m. to 2:00 p.m.), so v_avg = Δx/Δt = 60 km/h toward Q for each car.

questions.q: The diagram shows the motion of a toy car along a straight track. The car starts at the point marked start, moves to the right, turns around, and stops at the point marked finish. What is the car's displacement from start to finish?
optionWhy: A student who subtracts the final position from the initial one, x_0 − x = 10 m − (−15 m), picks this. A change is final minus initial; the car ends to the left of where it started, so Δx is negative.
Displacement is the change in position: Δx = x − x_0 = (−15 m) − (+10 m) = −25 m. The trip out to x = 20 m and back does not matter; only the start and finish positions do.
A student who takes the final position as the displacement picks this. −15 m is where the car ends up, measured from the origin; the car started at +10 m, so its displacement is (−15 m) − (+10 m).
A student who gives the distance traveled picks this: 10 m out to the turning point plus 35 m back. Displacement is a vector that depends only on the start and finish positions.
questions.explain: Displacement is the change in position: Δx = x − x_0 = (−15 m) − (+10 m) = −25 m. The trip out to x = 20 m and back does not matter; only the start and finish positions do.
questions.working: x_0 = +10 m and x = −15 m. Δx = x − x_0 = (−15 m) − (+10 m) = −25 m. (Distance traveled = 10 m out to x = 20 m + 35 m back = 45 m.)

questions.q: A cart moves up a straight ramp, slowing down at a steady rate. It turns around at its highest point and then speeds up at the same steady rate as it rolls back down. The direction up the ramp is positive. Which description matches the cart's velocity–time graph?
options: A straight line down to the time axis, then a straight line back up
A single straight line that slopes downward and crosses the time axis
A line that rises to a peak and then falls, just as the cart does
A line down to the time axis, then a flat part along the axis
optionWhy: A student who plots the speed rather than the velocity picks this. After the turning point the cart moves down the ramp, the negative direction, so its velocity is negative and grows in size below the axis; the graph does not bounce back up.

The velocity starts positive (up the ramp) and decreases at a steady rate to zero at the turning point, then keeps decreasing at the same rate, becoming more and more negative (down the ramp). One constant slope and a change of sign give one straight line that passes through the time axis.

A student who reads the graph as a picture of the cart going up and coming down picks this. The height of a velocity–time graph is the velocity, which is greatest at the start and decreases steadily: the graph never rises.

A student who thinks the cart rests for a while at the top picks this. The cart's velocity is zero for only an instant; the same steady change continues through the turning point, so there is no flat part.
questions.explain: The velocity starts positive (up the ramp) and decreases at a steady rate to zero at the turning point, then keeps decreasing at the same rate, becoming more and more negative (down the ramp). One constant slope and a change of sign give one straight line that passes through the time axis.

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward, reaches its highest point, and falls back down. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement correctly compares the ball's acceleration at different stages of its flight?
options: It is upward while the ball rises and downward while the ball falls back down.
It is downward and the same size while rising, at the top, and while falling.
It is downward while rising and while falling, but it is zero at the highest point.
It is downward throughout, but it is smallest near the top, where the ball is slowest.
optionWhy: A student who thinks acceleration points in the direction of motion picks this. While rising, the ball slows down, so its velocity change is downward: the acceleration is downward on the way up as well.

Near Earth's surface the only influence on the ball is gravity, so its acceleration is g, downward and constant, at every stage. At the top the velocity is momentarily zero but is still changing from upward to downward.

A student who thinks zero velocity means zero acceleration picks this. At the top the velocity is zero for only an instant; it is still changing at 10 m/s each second, so the acceleration there is still g downward.

A student who links the size of the acceleration to the speed picks this. The velocity changes by the same amount each second at every stage, however slowly the ball is moving, so the acceleration has the same size throughout.
questions.explain: Near Earth's surface the only influence on the ball is gravity, so its acceleration is g, downward and constant, at every stage. At the top the velocity is momentarily zero but is still changing from upward to downward.

questions.q: An object falls freely near Earth's surface. Air resistance is negligible. Use g = 10 m/s². Which statement about the object's motion is correct?
options: It falls through a distance of 10 m during each second of its fall.
Its acceleration is greater than 10 m/s² if it has a large mass.
Its velocity changes by 10 m/s downward during each second of its fall.
Its acceleration increases as its speed increases during the fall.
optionWhy: A student who reads 10 m/s² as '10 m every second' picks this. The unit means the VELOCITY changes by 10 m/s each second. The distances fallen in successive seconds from rest are 5 m, 15 m, 25 m …, not a steady 10 m.
A student who thinks heavier objects fall faster picks this. With air resistance negligible, every object near Earth's surface falls with the same acceleration, g, whatever its mass.
An acceleration of 10 m/s² downward means the velocity changes by 10 m/s downward in every second: from rest, 0, 10, 20, 30 m/s downward at 0, 1, 2, 3 s.
A student who links the size of the acceleration to the speed picks this. The speed does increase, but by the same 10 m/s every second, so the acceleration stays constant at 10 m/s².
questions.explain: An acceleration of 10 m/s² downward means the velocity changes by 10 m/s downward in every second: from rest, 0, 10, 20, 30 m/s downward at 0, 1, 2, 3 s.
questions.working: a = g = 10 m/s² downward: Δv = aΔt = 10 m/s per 1 s. From rest, distances in successive 1 s intervals: (1/2)(10)(1)² = 5 m, (1/2)(10)(2)² − 5 = 15 m, 45 − 20 = 25 m.

questions.q: The motion diagram shows the position of a cart at six instants separated by equal time intervals, as the cart moves to the right along a straight track. The dots are numbered in time order. Which claim about the cart's acceleration is supported by the diagram?
options: It points to the right, since the cart moves to the right during the whole time shown.
It is zero, since the cart is slowing down rather than speeding up as it goes.
It points to the left, since the cart moves a shorter distance in each interval.
It is decreasing in size, since the gaps between the dots get smaller and smaller.
optionWhy: A student who thinks acceleration points in the direction of motion picks this. The cart does move to the right, but it covers less distance in each interval, so its velocity is decreasing: the velocity change, and so the acceleration, points to the left.
A student who thinks 'acceleration' means only speeding up picks this. Slowing down is a change in velocity too, so the cart has a nonzero acceleration, directed opposite to its motion (to the left).

The gaps between successive dots are 5 m, 4 m, 3 m, 2 m and 1 m. Equal time intervals with shrinking gaps mean the cart's velocity to the right is decreasing, so the change in velocity, and hence the acceleration, points to the left. (Each gap is 1 m shorter than the one before, so the acceleration is constant.)

A student who links the size of the acceleration to the speed picks this. Smaller gaps show a smaller VELOCITY. Each gap is exactly 1 m shorter than the one before, so the velocity drops by the same amount in every interval: the acceleration is constant, not decreasing.
questions.explain: The gaps between successive dots are 5 m, 4 m, 3 m, 2 m and 1 m. Equal time intervals with shrinking gaps mean the cart's velocity to the right is decreasing, so the change in velocity, and hence the acceleration, points to the left. (Each gap is 1 m shorter than the one before, so the acceleration is constant.)
questions.working: Gaps: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 m in equal time intervals. The displacement per interval (average velocity) falls by 1 m each interval, so the velocity to the right decreases at a steady rate: acceleration constant and directed to the left.

questions.q: A train moves forward along a straight, level track at a constant 20 m/s. A passenger walks toward the back of the train. A seated passenger measures her velocity as 1.5 m/s toward the back of the train. A person standing on the platform measures her velocity as 18.5 m/s forward. Which statement about these two measurements is correct?
options: Both are correct, since each is measured relative to a different frame.
The platform value is the true one, since the platform is at rest.
The train value is the true one, since it is the velocity of her own walking.
They cannot both be correct, since they give opposite directions.
optionWhy: A velocity is always measured relative to a frame. Relative to the train she moves at 1.5 m/s toward the back; the train carries her forward at 20 m/s, so relative to the platform she moves at −1.5 m/s + 20 m/s = 18.5 m/s forward. Each observer's value is correct for that observer's frame.

A student who treats the ground as the one true frame picks this. The platform is at rest only in the ground's own frame; the seated passenger's measurement is just as valid, and it is the velocity that passenger actually observes.

A student who thinks the motion an object produces itself is its real motion picks this. Her walking velocity is simply her velocity relative to the train floor; relative to the platform the train's motion must be included, and that value is equally correct.

A student who thinks direction of motion belongs to the object itself picks this. Direction is measured relative to a frame: she moves toward the back relative to the train and forward relative to the platform, and both statements are true.
questions.explain: A velocity is always measured relative to a frame. Relative to the train she moves at 1.5 m/s toward the back; the train carries her forward at 20 m/s, so relative to the platform she moves at −1.5 m/s + 20 m/s = 18.5 m/s forward. Each observer's value is correct for that observer's frame.
questions.working: Train frame: 1.5 m/s backward (−1.5 m/s, forward positive). Ground frame: −1.5 m/s + 20 m/s = +18.5 m/s. Both values follow from the same motion; each is her velocity relative to a different frame.

questions.q: A glass elevator moves upward at a constant 3 m/s. A passenger in the elevator holds a coin at rest relative to the elevator and then releases it. Air resistance is negligible. An observer standing on the ground outside watches the coin until it lands on the elevator floor. Which statement about the coin's acceleration is correct?
options: The ground observer measures it upward at first, while the coin is rising.
The ground observer measures it as zero when the coin stops rising.
Both measure the same acceleration, g downward, throughout the flight.
The passenger measures a larger one, since the elevator moves upward.
optionWhy: A student who thinks acceleration points along the motion picks this. The ground observer does see the coin rise at first, but it is slowing down, so its change in velocity, and its acceleration, is downward.

A student who thinks zero velocity means zero acceleration picks this. At the top of its rise the coin's velocity is zero for only an instant and is still changing, so its acceleration there is still g downward.

The elevator moves at constant velocity, so its frame is inertial. The two observers' velocities for the coin always differ by the same 3 m/s, so the change in velocity each second, and hence the acceleration, is g downward for both, at every instant.

A student who thinks acceleration depends on the observer's velocity, like velocity itself, picks this. A constant elevator velocity shifts every measured velocity by the same amount and leaves the acceleration unchanged.
questions.explain: The elevator moves at constant velocity, so its frame is inertial. The two observers' velocities for the coin always differ by the same 3 m/s, so the change in velocity each second, and hence the acceleration, is g downward for both, at every instant.
questions.working: Both frames are inertial (ground at rest, elevator at constant velocity). Passenger: coin starts at rest and falls; ground: coin starts at 3 m/s upward, rises 0.45 m, stops momentarily and falls. In both frames the velocity changes by g downward each second, so both measure g downward throughout.

questions.q: A ball rests on level ground. Several observers move along the ground in straight lines at constant velocity. Which observer measures the ball's velocity as 5 m/s to the left?
options: An observer moving left at 5 m/s
No observer, since the ball is at rest
An observer moving right at 5 m/s
Any observer moving at 5 m/s either way
optionWhy: A student who subtracts in the wrong order, finding the observer's velocity relative to the ball, picks this. An observer moving left at 5 m/s measures 0 − (−5 m/s) = +5 m/s: the ball appears to move to the right.

A student who thinks being at rest is a property of the ball itself picks this. The ball is at rest relative to the ground only; an observer moving relative to the ground measures a nonzero velocity for it.

The velocity an observer measures is the object's velocity minus the observer's velocity. With right positive, 0 − (+5 m/s) = −5 m/s: an observer moving right at 5 m/s sees the ball move left at 5 m/s, just as a passenger sees roadside objects move backward.

A student who combines speeds and ignores directions picks this. The direction of the observer's motion decides the direction measured: moving right gives 5 m/s to the left, but moving left gives 5 m/s to the right.
questions.explain: The velocity an observer measures is the object's velocity minus the observer's velocity. With right positive, 0 − (+5 m/s) = −5 m/s: an observer moving right at 5 m/s sees the ball move left at 5 m/s, just as a passenger sees roadside objects move backward.
questions.working: Ground frame, right positive: ball v = 0. Observer with velocity u measures 0 − u = −u. For −5 m/s (5 m/s to the left), u = +5 m/s: the observer moves right at 5 m/s.

questions.q: A moving walkway in an airport moves at constant velocity v_W relative to the floor. A passenger walks on the walkway with velocity v_P relative to the walkway. A worker walks on the floor beside the walkway at constant velocity v_F relative to the floor. All three velocities are components along the same straight line. Which expression gives the passenger's velocity as measured by the worker?
options: v_P − v_W − v_F
v_P + v_W + v_F
v_F − v_P − v_W
v_P + v_W − v_F
optionWhy: A student who subtracts the frame's velocity at every change of frame picks this. Converting from the walkway to the floor needs v_W ADDED: a passenger standing still on the walkway moves at +v_W relative to the floor, not −v_W.

A student who always adds velocities picks this. The worker's own velocity must be subtracted: a worker walking beside the passenger at the same velocity should measure zero, which this expression does not give.
A student who subtracts in the wrong order picks this. This is the worker's velocity relative to the passenger, which has the same magnitude as the answer but the opposite sign.

Relative to the floor, the passenger moves at v_P + v_W, since the walkway carries everything on it at v_W. The worker measures that velocity minus the worker's own velocity relative to the floor: v_P + v_W − v_F. A worker keeping pace with the passenger measures zero, as expected.
questions.explain: Relative to the floor, the passenger moves at v_P + v_W, since the walkway carries everything on it at v_W. The worker measures that velocity minus the worker's own velocity relative to the floor: v_P + v_W − v_F. A worker keeping pace with the passenger measures zero, as expected.
questions.working: Step 1, walkway frame to floor frame: add the walkway's velocity, v_P,floor = v_P + v_W. Step 2, floor frame to worker's frame: subtract the worker's velocity, v_P,worker = (v_P + v_W) − v_F. Check: if the worker walks beside the passenger at the same floor velocity, v_F = v_P + v_W and the result is 0.

questions.q: A cart moves up a straight ramp inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Student 1 resolves the cart's velocity into horizontal and vertical components. Student 2 resolves the same velocity using an x-axis along the ramp and a y-axis perpendicular to the ramp. Which statement about their results is correct?
options: Their components must match, since both pairs describe one velocity.
Their components differ, but each pair combines to give the same velocity.
Student 2's are not proper components, as components are horizontal and vertical.
Their components differ, so the two students find different speeds.
optionWhy: A student who thinks components are fixed properties of the vector picks this. The components depend on the chosen axes; the same velocity has components (v cos 30°, v sin 30°) in one system and (v, 0) in the other.

Components depend on the axes chosen. Student 1 finds two nonzero components, v cos 30° and v sin 30°; Student 2, with an axis along the motion, finds v and 0. Each pair is a correct description: combined, both give the same vector, with the same speed v up the ramp.
A student who thinks components must be horizontal and vertical picks this. Any pair of perpendicular axes can be used; axes along the ramp are often the most convenient choice here.

A student who thinks the magnitude depends on the axes picks this. Both pairs give the same magnitude: (v cos 30°)² + (v sin 30°)² = v², and v² + 0² = v². The speed does not depend on the coordinate system.
questions.explain: Components depend on the axes chosen. Student 1 finds two nonzero components, v cos 30° and v sin 30°; Student 2, with an axis along the motion, finds v and 0. Each pair is a correct description: combined, both give the same vector, with the same speed v up the ramp.
questions.working: Speed v up the ramp. Student 1: v_x = v cos 30°, v_y = v sin 30° (both nonzero). Student 2: v_x′ = v, v_y′ = 0. The pairs differ, but √((v cos 30°)² + (v sin 30°)²) = v = √(v² + 0²): same vector, same speed.

questions.q: Ball A, of mass 2m, is launched horizontally from the edge of a table at the same instant that ball B, of mass m, is released from rest at the same height. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement correctly compares the times at which the two balls reach the floor?
options: Ball A lands together with B, as their vertical motions match.
Ball A lands later, as its horizontal motion helps to hold it up.
Ball A lands first, as its greater mass makes it fall faster.
Ball A lands later, as it starts to fall once its forward motion dies.
optionWhy: Separate each motion into components. Vertically, both balls start with zero vertical velocity, fall through the same height and accelerate at g whatever their mass, so they reach the floor together. A's horizontal velocity only carries it farther sideways.
A student who thinks sideways motion keeps a projectile aloft picks this. With air resistance negligible, A's vertical acceleration is g, the same as B's, whatever its horizontal velocity.
A student who thinks heavier objects fall faster picks this. With air resistance negligible, both balls have the same downward acceleration, g, whatever their masses.

A student who thinks a launched ball moves forward until its 'impetus' is used up, and then falls, picks this. A starts to fall at the instant it leaves the table, and its horizontal velocity does not die away.
questions.explain: Separate each motion into components. Vertically, both balls start with zero vertical velocity, fall through the same height and accelerate at g whatever their mass, so they reach the floor together. A's horizontal velocity only carries it farther sideways.
questions.working: Vertical motion of each ball: v_y0 = 0, a_y = −g (independent of mass and of horizontal velocity), same drop h, so both take t = √(2h/g).

questions.q: A ball is launched at an angle above the horizontal from level ground. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement describes the ball's acceleration at the highest point of its path?
options: It is g, directed downward, the same as at every other point of the path.
It is zero, since the ball stops rising and moves horizontally there.
It is horizontal, pointing the way the ball is moving at that point.
It is less than g, since the ball's horizontal motion helps hold it up.
optionWhy: A projectile's acceleration is g downward at every point of its path. At the highest point v_y is zero for an instant but is still changing, from upward to downward, at the same rate as everywhere else, while v_x does not change at all.
A student who thinks the acceleration is zero at the highest point picks this. v_y is zero there for only an instant and is still changing by g each second, so the acceleration is still g downward.

A student who thinks acceleration points along the direction of motion picks this. The ball's velocity is horizontal at the top, but only its vertical component is changing, so the acceleration is vertical, g downward.
A student who thinks sideways motion keeps a projectile aloft picks this. With air resistance negligible the vertical acceleration is g whatever the horizontal velocity.
questions.explain: A projectile's acceleration is g downward at every point of its path. At the highest point v_y is zero for an instant but is still changing, from upward to downward, at the same rate as everywhere else, while v_x does not change at all.

questions.q: A robot vacuum moves 1.1 m east and then 1.6 m north, each along a straight line. What is the magnitude of its displacement from its starting point?
optionWhy: A student who adds the two distances as ordinary numbers, 1.1 m + 1.6 m, picks this. That is the distance traveled; the displacement is the resultant of two perpendicular components and must be found with a² + b² = c².
A student who stops at 1.1² + 1.6² = 3.77 and forgets the square root picks this. That number is c² in m²; the displacement is its square root, 1.9 m.
The east and north displacements are perpendicular components of the total displacement, which is the hypotenuse of the right triangle they form: √((1.1 m)² + (1.6 m)²) = √(3.77 m²) = 1.9 m.
A student who treats the longer displacement, 1.6 m, as the hypotenuse and calculates √(1.6² − 1.1²) picks this. The resultant is the hypotenuse; both given displacements are the perpendicular sides.
questions.explain: The east and north displacements are perpendicular components of the total displacement, which is the hypotenuse of the right triangle they form: √((1.1 m)² + (1.6 m)²) = √(3.77 m²) = 1.9 m.
questions.working: The two displacements are perpendicular components of the total displacement. |Δr| = √(1.1² + 1.6²) m = √(1.21 + 2.56) m = √3.77 m = 1.9 m (1.94 m).
